Questions answered from the MAP only are made by the page from the map itself (a square, the place of a kind in a square, a direction, a key symbol). `blanks`: two places whose names the page hides on level 3. `diagrams`: three paragraphs, a diagram of four steps with library pictures (a chain or a cycle), and questions answered from the DIAGRAM only, the TEXT only, or BOTH; `says` = what happens in a step (the sample answer of the level 3 task "write the missing step"). `find`: the words of the text that prove an answer given in other words; `cue`: the words of a BOTH question that only the text explains; `group`: two questions of one group never stand on one page (one would give the other away); `via: "diagram"`: a both question that points at a step by its place in the diagram.

maps.title: The Railroad Across America
parts: In the 1860s, a trip across the United States by wagon took many months.
People wanted a railroad that would join the two sides of the country.
In 1863, two railroad companies began to build it.
The Central Pacific Railroad started in Sacramento, California.
Its workers dug tunnels through the tall, rocky Sierra Nevada mountains.
The Union Pacific Railroad started in Omaha, Nebraska.
Its workers laid track across wide, flat grassland and then over the Rocky Mountains.
The work was hard and often dangerous.
On May 10, 1869, the two railroads met at Promontory Summit, Utah.
A golden spike was tapped into the last tie to mark the finish.
News of it was sent across the country by telegraph.
After that, a trip across the country took only about a week.

maps.title: The Mighty Mississippi
parts: The Mississippi River is one of the longest rivers in North America.
It begins as a small, clear stream that flows out of Lake Itasca in Minnesota.
There, the river is so narrow that people can walk across it on stepping stones.
The river winds along for about 2,350 miles.
In Minneapolis, it tumbles over a waterfall called St. Anthony Falls.
Other big rivers pour into it on the way.
The Missouri River joins it near the city of St. Louis.
Farther down, the Ohio River joins it at the town of Cairo, Illinois.
With all this water, the Mississippi grows wide and deep.
Today, long, flat boats called barges travel on the river.
They carry corn, coal, and other goods.
The river ends where it empties into the sea, past the city of New Orleans.

maps.title: The National Mall
parts: The National Mall is a long, grassy park in Washington, D.C.
Famous buildings and memorials stand along it.
A memorial is built to help people remember a person or an event.
Millions of people visit the Mall every year.
At one end of the Mall is the U.S. Capitol, where Congress meets to make the country's laws.
At the other end is the Lincoln Memorial.
Inside it, a giant statue of Abraham Lincoln sits in a chair and looks out over a long pool of water.
Between them rises the Washington Monument, a tall stone tower that honors George Washington, the first president.
It is about 555 feet tall.
The White House, where the president lives, is not far away.
So is the Jefferson Memorial, which stands beside a small lake called the Tidal Basin.

maps.title: The Iditarod Sled Dog Race
parts: Every March, teams of sled dogs race across Alaska in the Iditarod.
Each team has a driver, called a musher, and a group of strong, fast dogs.
The musher stands on the back of the sled.
The trail is about 1,000 miles long.
The race starts in the city of Anchorage.
The teams cross frozen rivers, thick forests, and tall mountains.
Along the trail, they stop at places called checkpoints.
Most are in small villages.
There the mushers rest, and the dogs eat and get checked by animal doctors.
One checkpoint is Unalakleet, a village near the sea.
The race ends in the town of Nome.
It honors a famous trip in 1925, when sled dog teams carried medicine to Nome to help sick children.
The fastest teams finish in about nine days.

maps.title: Yellowstone National Park
parts: Yellowstone became the first national park in the world in 1872.
Most of the park is in Wyoming, and small parts are in Montana and Idaho.
It has more than 10,000 hot springs, mud pots, and geysers.
A geyser is a hot spring that shoots water and steam high into the air.
The most famous geyser in the park is Old Faithful.
It erupts about every hour and a half, many times every day.
Norris Geyser Basin is the hottest place in the park.
At Mammoth Hot Springs, hot water has built steps of white stone.
Near Canyon, a waterfall called the Lower Falls drops more than 300 feet.
Yellowstone Lake is the biggest lake in North America that sits more than 7,000 feet up in the mountains.
Herds of bison roam across the wide, grassy valleys.

diagrams.title: Water on the Move
parts: The water on Earth is always on the move.
It goes up into the sky and comes back down, over and over again.
The water you drink today may have fallen as rain long, long ago.
Heat from the sun warms the water in oceans, lakes, and rivers.
Some of the water turns into a gas called water vapor, which you cannot see.
The vapor rises high into the sky, where the air is cold.
There it cools and turns back into tiny drops of water.
Many tiny drops together make a cloud.
When the drops in a cloud bump together, they grow big and heavy.
Then they fall to the ground as rain, or as snow when the air is very cold.
The water runs into rivers, lakes, and oceans, and the trip begins again.

diagrams.title: Energy in a Food Chain
parts: Every living thing needs energy to grow, move, and stay alive.
A food chain shows how energy passes from one living thing to another.
Almost every food chain on Earth starts with energy from the sun.
Plants can make their own food.
They use sunlight, water, and air to make it.
A plant stores this energy in its leaves, stems, and roots.
Animals cannot make food, so they must eat.
Animals that eat only plants are called herbivores.
Some animals hunt and eat other animals.
Animals that hunt are called predators.
The animals they hunt are called their prey.
When an animal eats, it gets the energy that was stored in its food.
In this way, energy moves along the chain.

diagrams.title: Food Chains in the Ocean
parts: The ocean is full of food chains, just like the land.
Many ocean food chains begin with living things that use sunlight to make their own food.
Sunlight reaches only the top part of the ocean, so these food makers grow near the surface.
Some ocean animals eat only these food makers.
They graze on them slowly, the way cows graze on grass.
They give energy to the animals that eat them.
Other ocean animals are hunters with sharp teeth or strong jaws.
At the top of many ocean food chains are big hunters.
Few other animals can catch and eat them.
When ocean animals die, tiny living things called decomposers break down their bodies.
This puts nutrients back into the water, and the food makers use them to grow.

diagrams.title: How a Letter Travels
parts: When you mail a letter, it goes on a trip.
First, you write the address and the ZIP code on the envelope.
A ZIP code is a number that tells which town or part of a city the letter is going to.
A stamp in the corner pays for the trip.
Next, you drop the letter into a mailbox.
Later, it is picked up and taken to a big sorting center full of machines.
The machines read the ZIP code and sort the letters by where they are going.
A machine can sort thousands of letters in an hour.
Then the letters travel to a building near each address.
Last, a worker brings each letter to the right home.
Many letters get there in just a few days.

diagrams.title: How Animals Plant Trees
parts: Trees cannot walk, but many trees need to send their seeds to new places.
A seed that lands right under its parent tree gets little sunlight and water.
Wind and water carry some seeds away.
Animals carry others.
In the fall, some trees drop nuts, which are seeds with a hard shell.
Some animals gather the nuts and bury them in the ground, one here and one there.
In the winter, when food is hard to find, they dig up the nuts and eat them.
But the animals do not find every nut they hide.
In the spring, some of the forgotten nuts sprout.
Over many years, they can grow into big new trees, far from the parent tree.
In this way, a hungry animal helps a forest grow.
